paragraphs.source_en: Though one calls it washing their faces, the two older girls were only just attending kindergarten, and the third was so small she could hardly toddle along behind her sisters; naturally, they could not wash their faces in any proper manner, much less use cosmetics correctly. The smallest one dragged a wet rag out of a tin bucket and rubbed it industriously all over her face. Washing one's face with a rag must surely feel unpleasant, but since this little creature cries out “How fun, how fun” whenever there is an earthquake, such conduct is hardly surprising. In one sense, she may be even more detached from worldly concerns than Mr. Yagi Dokusen. The eldest girl, being the eldest after all, had appointed herself the elder sister; seeing this, she dropped her rinsing cup and said, “Little one, that's a rag.” So saying, she tried to take the rag away. The little one, however, was quite a confident soul herself and showed no wish to heed her sister, muttering, “No, babu.” She pulled the rag back again. What this “babu” means, or what its etymology may be, no one can determine; it is simply a word this little person often employs when angry. The rag was now being tugged back and forth between the sister and the little one, and the water it held dripped patter-patter from its middle all over the little one's feet; not content with her feet, it soaked her knees as well. The little one was, for all that, wearing a “Genroku.” When I made careful inquiries as to what “Genroku” meant, I learned that any cloth dyed with a medium-sized pattern was apparently called Genroku; who had taught this elder sister the word I do not know, but she said, “Little one, stop pulling, you'll get your Genroku wet.” This elder sister was very fond of using fresh new words; in fact, this learned young lady had until quite recently still confused “Genroku” with “sugoroku.”

paragraphs.source_en: Since Genroku has come up, I shall say a few words in passing. This child is constantly getting words wrong. At times she utters such mistaken expressions that one hardly knows whether to laugh or cry. At a fire she talks of “mushrooms flying through the sky”; sometimes she says she has gone to the Ocha “sauce” Girls' School instead of Ochanomizu Girls' School, and sometimes she puts Ebisu and the kitchen together. Once she even said, “I'm not a child from the straw shop,” and when questioned closely it turned out she had confused a back-street tenement with a straw shop. Whenever my master hears one of these mistakes, he laughs. Yet when he goes to school to teach English, he himself must surely be making even more comical errors than these, and presenting them to his students with perfect solemnity.

paragraphs.source_en: The little one, who does not call herself “little one” but always calls herself “Booba,” saw that the Genroku was wet, said something like “Gen-doko is cold,” and burst into tears. A cold, wet Genroku would never do, so the maid Osan hurried out from the kitchen, took the rag from the little one's hand, and wiped her clothes. The relatively quiet party amid this commotion was the second daughter, Miss Sunko; with her back turned, she had opened the bottle of face powder that had rolled down from the shelf and was busily adorning herself. First, with the finger she had thrust into the bottle, she drew a firm stroke down the tip of her nose, whereupon a single vertical white streak appeared and the location of her nose became rather clearly marked. Next she turned that powdered finger to her cheeks and rubbed it back and forth, and in consequence two large white patches immediately formed there as well. Just as her adornment was more or less complete, Osan came in to wipe the little one's clothes and, while she was about it, wiped the powder off Sunko's face too. Sunko appeared somewhat dissatisfied.

paragraphs.source_en: After watching this scene from the side, I went back through the sitting room to my master's bedroom and quietly looked in to see whether he had risen. When I looked, my master's head was nowhere to be seen; instead, one large, high-instepped foot was sticking out from under the bedding. No doubt he thought that if his head were showing, he would be troubled by someone calling him to get up, and so he had burrowed in like this. He was just like a turtle withdrawing its head. At this point, his wife, having finished cleaning the study, came back again carrying a broom and a duster, and, just as before, called from the entrance at the sliding screens:
